title: A Ledger for the Letter
premise: In the final winter of the Great War, battlefield nurse Tamsin Amberdale keeps a hidden ledger recording the names of dead soldiers that official reports omit—men erased by clerical error, desertion stigma, or deliberate cover-up. When census taker Edmund Voss arrives at her field hospital and stumbles onto the ledger, he must choose between reporting her and helping her smuggle it past three military checkpoints to a war correspondent before the armistice renders every unrecorded name permanently invisible. Along the way, the two strangers and the nurses, drivers, and wounded men who shelter them become an unlikely family bound by shared risk. The ledger reaches print hours after the armistice is signed—not in time to change the war, but in time to change who gets remembered by it.
about_author: Ulyana Montrose is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unsent letters from the First World War. She writes historical fiction about the people history filed under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: What the Orders Weigh
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. In a freezing casualty clearing station, she begins recording names of the dead that the morning reports omit, hiding the ledger inside a ration crate. Emotional beat: quiet defiance born of grief after losing a whole ward in one night.

chapters.title: The Man Who Counts Doors
chapters.summary: Edmund Voss's POV. A meticulous census taker arrives to count personnel at the clearing station, annoyed at his posting and hungry for a promotion. He notices discrepancies between headcounts and grave markers. Emotional beat: curiosity curdling into suspicion.

chapters.title: A Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. During his interview with Tamsin, he asks why the numbers don't reconcile; she deflects, but he glimpses the ledger's corner. Emotional beat: the first spark of complicity—he says nothing, and hates himself for it.

chapters.title: Names in Chalk
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Flashback chapter to her brother, listed as 'missing' though she watched him die, explaining why the ledger exists. Emotional beat: the wound beneath the discipline; memory as both burden and duty.

chapters.title: The Ration Crate Confession
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Edmund confronts Tamsin privately; instead of reporting her, he asks to read one page—and finds his own cousin's name among the omitted. Emotional beat: shock, then a bargain struck in whispers.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints, One Truth
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She learns the armistice may come within weeks; once peace is signed, the records will be sealed and shipped. She maps the route to correspondent Ada Quill in Amiens: the aid convoy gate, the rail yard, the press office. Emotional beat: fear sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Convoy Gate
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. First checkpoint: a suspicious transport officer cross-references manifests while the ledger hides in a wounded man's kit. Emotional beat: terror disguised as bureaucracy; Edmund discovers he can lie well, which frightens him.

chapters.title: Sister Brightwater's Kitchen
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Head nurse Brightwater, who has quietly known about the ledger for months, feeds the fugitives and offers her dead sister's identity papers as backup. Emotional beat: found family crystallizing around a pot of weak tea.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Carried It
chapters.summary: Orderly Pip Halloway's POV. Sixteen-year-old Pip volunteers to carry the ledger through the rail yard because no one searches a boy pushing a stretcher. Emotional beat: youthful bravado cracking into real courage under shellfire.

chapters.title: Rail Yard, 4 A.M.
chapters.summary: Pip's POV. Second checkpoint: a military policeman detains Pip over a forged pass; Tamsin talks her way through by claiming the boy is her patient. Emotional beat: near-loss, and the moment Pip stops being a child in her eyes.

chapters.title: What Voss Reports
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. His superior demands a full census report; Edmund submits accurate counts everywhere except the clearing station, falsifying his life's work. Emotional beat: self-betrayal as moral awakening—he becomes what he counted.

chapters.title: The Armistice Rumor
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. News spreads that signing may happen within days—or be delayed indefinitely. A rival matron denounces 'irregular record-keeping,' and an inspection is ordered. Emotional beat: the clock tightening; hope and dread in the same breath.

chapters.title: Inspection at Dawn
chapters.summary: Brightwater's POV. The matron searches the wards while the ledger sits in plain sight, disguised as a hymnal on the chapel shelf. Emotional beat: stillness as suspense; Brightwater's serenity masking mortal stakes.

chapters.title: Chapel Shelf
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The inspection passes by inches, but the matron posts a guard on all outgoing mail and parcels. The old routes are dead. Emotional beat: despair, then Tamsin's realization that the third checkpoint—the press office—is also the least guarded.

chapters.title: Ada Quill's Waiting Room
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The war correspondent, blocked by censors for months, explains exactly what evidence she needs and how little time remains. Emotional beat: professional cynicism pierced by genuine belief when she reads a single page.

chapters.title: The Long Road to Amiens
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Tamsin and Edmund travel together under cover of escorting a discharged patient, trading confessions—her brother, his cousin, their separate cowardices. Emotional beat: intimacy forged by shared guilt; almost-love, deliberately unfinished.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Three
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Final checkpoint: the press censor recognizes Edmund from prewar London and offers him a deal—denounce the ledger publicly and walk free. Emotional beat: the climax of conscience; Edmund refuses, and is arrested.

chapters.title: Eleven Minutes Past Eleven
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. With Edmund detained, Tamsin walks the ledger into the press office herself as church bells announce the armistice is signed. Emotional beat: triumph hollowed by cost—the war ends, and he is still in a cell.

chapters.title: The Cell and the Column
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. In custody, Edmund hears soldiers reading Ada's published column aloud—the names, including his cousin's. His interrogator, moved, tears up the charge sheet. Emotional beat: vindication arriving not as victory but as witness.

chapters.title: Reckonings
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She returns to the clearing station, where the matron who hunted the ledger reads the column in silence and, wordlessly, hands Tamsin back her confiscated letters. Emotional beat: grace from an enemy; grief finally allowed to speak.

chapters.title: A Ledger Closed, A Door Opened
chapters.summary: Brightwater's POV. The found family gathers—Tamsin, Edmund released, Pip, Ada—to decide what comes next: testifying at the records inquiry so the omissions become official corrections. Emotional beat: belonging chosen, not inherited.

chapters.title: Carry What Remains
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, epilogue. A year later, at a small village memorial where corrected names are read aloud, Tamsin closes the ledger and opens a blank notebook. Emotional beat: memory passed forward; the story ends where remembering begins.
